newsitem.title: UK: LME MARKETS END MIXED, PRICES HOPPING AROUND.
newsitem.headline: LME MARKETS END MIXED, PRICES HOPPING AROUND.

text.p: Base metals ended another LME session of random price movements mixed, with most markets able to rally off their lows without showing any sign of sustaining a definite trend, traders said.

Price movements were largely influenced by technical considerations, and with trade interest at a low ebb at this time of the year the speculative side of the market currently has the upper hand, they said.
"This is the summer period and there has not been much liquidity, certainly in copper, for some time now," analyst Martin Squires of LME trader Rudolf Wolff and Co said.
Copper whipped around between just below $2,300 and just above $2,260, thus remaining well within the well-worn range.
The market was resilient on the dips, with sentiment assisted by a constructive interpretation of the stock report -- a 50-tonne increase was seen as modest in the summer.
There was also little significant movement on the spreads, with the cash/threes backwardation remaining around $19. Last three months business was at $2,290 a tonne, up $12 from Tuesday.
Aluminium climbed off its $1,687 lows, but still ended easier and under $1,700. Last business was at $1,696, down $19.
Some said that the 4,100-tonne stock increase -- the second successive daily rise -- may herald a change in the inventory trend. But others said it was premature to suggest stock falls had now ended.
"It is too early to say...I would like to see a good week or so of stock rises," Squires said.
Some metal may also have been attracted to warehouses by the backwardation, which although softer on Wednesday, could spike out next week when the August date is traded.

Zinc managed to stage a recovery from depressed midsession levels, pulled up by the trend in copper and aluminium. However, the upturn still left prices adrift of $1,500 overhead, closing $5 firmer at $1,485.

In the short-term business will remain volatile as the market tries to gauge the severity of the upcoming tightness. On Wednesday, spread backwardations softened, with some lending seen, with the cash/threes last indicated at $105/$115.
Meanwhile, stock trends are difficult to call at present. There was a 4,475-tonne stock fall today, but the bulk of the decline was due to a near 5,000-tonne shipment out of Rotterdam.
The net rise in Singapore was 575 tonnes, and traders expect further sizeable tonnages to be delivered there.
Nickel prices fell away during the afternoon, as sell-stops were hit when chart support levels were breached.
Earlier, a 690-tonne stock increase underlined current slow physicals and ample availability of metal. Last business was at $6,510, down $190 from Tuesday.
Lead was steady throughout the session, largely paying little heed to the fluctuations elsewhere as the market corrected above $600 and the new 22-month low hit on Tuesday.
Traders said, however, that the respite may be temporary, with charts bearish. Prices finished at $607, up $10.
Tin moved off its lows, and closed at $5,410, down just $5. Alloy was at a little-changed $1,505/10.
--Martin Hayes, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8080
